Learning Objectives
Review the cellular mechanisms through which osteolysis from polyethylene wear occurs.
Identify risk factors for polyethylene wear.
Review manufacturing and sterilization techniques that affect the rate of polyethylene wear
and subsequent osteolysis.
Review the diagnosis, management, and complications associated with osteolysis resulting
from polyethylene wear.


Overview
Polyethylene is produced via the polymerization of ethylene gas into a macromolecular
carbon chain. Its incorporation in total hip arthroplasty (THA) was pioneered by Sir John
Charnley. Polyethylene wear, osteolysis, and related implant loosening fueled
improvements, including alterations to thermal processing, sterilization, and packaging.
The second-generation highly cross-linked polyethylene (HXLPE) has been the industry
standard since 2005.1
Osteolysis

Osteolysis
Osteolysis in THA implants is the result of cellular response to wear debris. It is most
commonly associated with polyethylene particles but may be observed with other wear
debris products, such as cement, metal, or ceramic particles2 The number, size, and
shape of the debris particles influence the biologic response and, consequently, the
amount of osteolysis. The problem was first described by Harris et al3 in 1976 as
extensive localized bone resorption around a cemented femoral stem. By the early
2000s, the incidence of osteolysis at 10 years was higher than the sum of all other
complications added together.4 Rates of osteolysis reached 60% in some series of
patients.4 Given the scope of the problem, alternative bearing surfaces were researched
and became popular. The introduction of HXLPE has considerably reduced the incidence
of osteolysis. This represented a substantial step forward in THA and a major
improvement over conventional polyethylene or ultra-high–molecular-weight
polyethylene (UHMWPE). A considerable reduction in the incidence of osteolysis is noted
at follow-up greater than 10 years.5
Clinical Importance of Osteolysis


Clinical Importance of Osteolysis
There is a strong association between higher wear rates of bearing surfaces and
osteolysis.2 Osteolysis can produce cavitary defects in the pelvis and the proximal femur.
These defects can result in fracture but more commonly result in aseptic loosening of
components in patients with extensive osteolysis. Clinical concerns in the 1990s
regarding osteolysis led surgeons and manufacturers to investigate alternative bearing
surfaces, which led to the resurgence of metal-on-metal and ceramic-on-ceramic
bearings.6 The popularization of HXLPE has contributed to the reduction in revision THA
performed for the management of aseptic loosening resulting from osteolysis, even for
metal-on-polyethylene bearings.7 In the Australian Orthopaedic Association National
Joint Replacement Registry, the 16-year cumulative percentage of revision THA in
patients in whom UHMWPE was implanted was 11.7% compared with 6.2% in patients in
whom cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE) was used. The difference can be attributed to the
reduction in rates of osteolysis, dislocation, and loosening.8 Metal head- or ceramic
head-on-polyethylene are the most common bearing surfaces used.
Basic Science

Basic Science
Surgeons must understand the cellular mechanisms through which osteolysis occurs.
Particles measuring 150 nm to 10 μm can be phagocytosed by cells. Monocytes are most
responsive to particles in the 0.21- to 7.2-μm range. Polyethylene debris particles often
are needlelike and typically range in size from 0.3 to 0.5 μm. Particles created from XLPE
are smaller than those from UHMWPE and can trigger a more robust immune response;
however, the volume of debris from XLPE is substantially lower. These particles mainly
interact with macrophages and trigger a foreign-body inflammatory response. Wear
debris also can negatively affect the ability of the body to lay down new bone. Debris can
induce mesenchymal stem cell apoptosis and/or block osteoblastic differentiation.9

The macrophage is the dominant cell involved in particle-mediated osteolysis because of
polyethylene debris. Multinucleated giant cells have been identified at the bone implant
interface of aseptically loosened implants because of advanced polyethylene wear. Their
presence contributes to osteoclast-driven bone resorption via the release of tumor
necrosis factor-α (TNF-α). The smaller particles released by XLPE have been shown to
induce a larger release of TNF-α from macrophages compared with UHMWPE; however,
the number of UHMWPE particles released is higher compared with the number of XLPE
particles released if all other variables are held constant. In a study in which
pseudocapsular tissue was sampled from patients undergoing revision THA, the mean
estimated number of particles per gram in the annealed XLPE group was four times
lower than that in the conventional polyethylene cohort (Figure 1; Video 1; Resources
1 and 2).

The Role of the Macrophage in Osteolysis
Macrophage activation can occur through phagocytosis or cell contact activation.
Cell contact activation is mediated through toll-like receptors (TLRs), specifically TLR2 and
TLR4. These mediators have been found to be important in polyethylene-induced osteolysis.
Debris-activated macrophages, through either TLRs or phagocytosis, increase transcription of
nuclear factor κ B; nuclear factor κ B has been shown to be a key factor in polyethylene-
induced osteolysis because this mediates the proinflammatory response.
In turn, nuclear factor κ B furthers the inflammatory response by inducing the release of

monocytes, and osteoclast precursor cells to the area of debris.

Risk Factors for Wear and Osteolysis
Most studies on polyethylene wear evaluated the performance of UHMWPE. Fewer studies
have been performed to study the performance of XLPE.
Patient factors (Table 1)
Activity level can vary greatly between patients. In counseling patients, particularly younger
and more active patients, discussion of the relationship between certain activities and
increased wear rates is important. A 2012 study compared patients with UHMWPE who
engaged in high-impact sports versus those with lower activity demands. Those in the high-
activity cohort demonstrated increased wear rates and lower survivorship. Osteolysis around
the femoral stem was observed in 15.7% of the high-impact cohort at final follow-up.10-12
More recent studies on XLPE have demonstrated reassuringly low wear rates in younger
patients. In a retrospective study of 89 THA procedures in patients with a mean age of 38.8
years, no evidence of osteolysis was noted at 15-year follow-up. Linear and volumetric wear
were clinically undetectable, and no wear-related revisions occurred.13

Implant factors (Resource 3)
Linear polyethylene wear rates have been shown to be independent of the size of the
femoral head;14 however, several studies have demonstrated increased volumetric wear
rates with larger (>32-mm outer diameter) femoral heads if used in combination with XLPE
liners.15-17 Data from the Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint Replacement
Registry demonstrate that larger diameter femoral heads do not increase the risk of long-
term wear-related adverse events.8
Earlier studies on UHMWPE demonstrated an association between polyethylene thickness
and wear, with liners thinner than 7 mm being associated with higher linear wear rates. This
led to a recommendation that liners should be thicker than 7 mm.18 More recent studies
with XLPE failed to show a relationship between liner thickness and wear rates;19,20 however,
liner thickness, particularly at the rim, has been shown to be a risk factor for liner fracture.
Retrieval studies have identified polyethylene thickness at the rim of the implant to be a risk
factor for liner fracture, particularly if the liner thickness is less than 4 mm.21-23
Dual mobility has gained popularity in primary and revision THA because good data support
reduction in dislocation and improved stability. The addition of another bearing surface
raises concern for increased wear because an additional articulation is present between the
dual-mobility insert and the acetabular shell. Retrieval studies of dual-mobility constructs
from France using UHMWPE demonstrated no increased wear compared with cementless
liners.24 Other retrieval studies on XLPE have demonstrated that wear occurs on both sides

of the liner but that more damage occurs at the femoral head–polyethylene liner interface
than at the liner-cup interface.25 Regardless, after the first year, the annual wear rate of dual-
mobility constructs is between 0.02 and 0.09 mm per year according to radiostereometric
analysis measurement and, therefore, below the 0.1-mm per year threshold for being at risk
for the development of osteolysis.26
Surgical considerations (Table 2)
Component positioning in THA can affect the contact stresses and, consequently, wear
experienced by the implants. An acetabular inclination greater than 45° was associated with
increased linear and volumetric wear in a series of 43 hips followed for a mean of 64
months27 because the load per unit area on the superior aspect of the polyethylene is
increased by the vertical position of the cup. In another study, increased linear wear rates
were noted with progressive increases in inclination. Increased rates of osteolysis also were
found.28
Increased abduction angles also have been associated with fatigue fracture at the rim of the
liner, particularly in XLPE liners, which have relatively reduced toughness compared with
UHMWPE liners.21,29
An inclination greater than 45° is associated with increased wear and peak contact stresses.
The location of maximal wear shifts superiorly as the abduction angle increases. An increase
in anteversion from 0° to 30° decreases peak contact stresses.30

Manufacturing Considerations to Prevent Wear

Manufacturing Considerations to Prevent Wear
Polyethylene is a repeating chain of ethylene molecules. XLPE refers to bonds formed by
carbon atoms between these long chains within the material. Most commonly, cross-
linking is achieved via irradiation, in which carbon-hydrogen bonds are disrupted and
free radicals are formed. Although many of these free radicals will bond to another chain
(cross-linking) in the presence of oxygen, some free radicals will bond to oxygen, leading
to oxidation of the material, which adversely affects the mechanical and wear properties.
If irradiation occurs in an inert gas or vacuum, the carbon atoms bind to each other
across chains without the risk of oxidation.
Cross-linking improves the wear properties at the expense of mechanical strength,
ductility, and fatigue resistance. After irradiation, the polyethylene is heated to eliminate
free radicals, with the goal of diminishing the likelihood for future oxidative degradation.
Melting occurs if the polyethylene is heated above its melting point. Annealing occurs if
the polyethylene is heated to just below the melting point. Melting is more effective at
eliminating free radicals; however, it does further compromise the mechanical
properties. In contrast, annealing eliminates fewer free radicals but largely maintains the
mechanical properties of the polymer. Vitamin E also is used as a biologic antioxidant
that neutralizes free radicals.31
Wear of UHMWPE Compared With XLPE


Wear of UHMWPE Compared With XLPE
Wear rates of greater than 0.1 mm per year are associated with the development of
osteolysis;2 below this threshold osteolysis either is not observed or is a rare occurrence.
A systematic review of XLPE found the mean femoral penetration to be 0.042 mm per
year.1 With UHMWPE, an annual rate of 0.137 mm per year was found.2 The estimated
reduction in wear rates comparing cross-linked and conventional polyethylene in studies
with a minimum follow-up of 5 years is approximately 72%.32,33 In a randomized trial,
patients received XLPE or conventional polyethylene, with all other implant
considerations held equal. At 15-year follow-up, wear-related revisions occurred in 12%
of patients implanted with conventional polyethylene compared with zero in the XLPE
cohort. Osteolysis was found in only 9% of XLPE patients compared with 46% in the
conventional cohort.34 In 2011, a meta-analysis assessed at the rates of osteolysis after
THA and calculated a relative risk reduction of 0.40 favoring XLPE compared with
UHMWPE35 (Video 2).

Monitoring for Osteolysis and Polyethylene Wear

Monitoring for Osteolysis and Polyethylene Wear
Polyethylene wear can be detected on plain weight-bearing radiographs. If sufficient
wear is present, the examiner will notice the femoral head seated eccentrically in the
acetabular component. Osteolysis in the absence of prosthetic loosening typically is not
associated with pain and, therefore, often is detected incidentally. Polyethylene wear is
an established risk factor for late dislocation, and the cumulative risk of hip dislocation
does increase over time.36,37In evaluating for osteolysis, Judet views may be helpful in
delineating the extent of the osteolysis; However, conventional radiographs may
underestimate the burden of osteolysis. Accordingly, CT and, to a greater extent, MRI,
with the appropriate metal subtraction protocols, may be more helpful in defining the
extent of osteolysis.38 Although CT and MRI are powerful tools for evaluating the extent
of osteolysis, radiostereometric analysis is considered the most accurate method of
measuring wear. However, this technique requires specialized equipment and the
implantation of tantalum beads at the time of surgery, which limits its widespread use.
Some studies have used radiostereometric analysis with off-the-shelf implants and have
achieved reasonable accuracy in measuring wear.39 Currently, no established biologic
measurements or assays are available to measure wear. Several biomarkers are under
investigation, but their clinical utility has not been established.40,41 (Resource 4)
Management of Osteolysis
After polyethylene wear is diagnosed, management consists of revision of the acetabular liner.
Indications for isolated liner exchange are narrow, and the procedure should not be performed if
the components are malpositioned, loose, or have a poor locking mechanism. The goals of
management include addressing the wear by replacing the polyethylene liner, reconstitution of

rates after polyethylene liner exchange have been reported to be as high as 30% in some
series43,44 and should be recognized as the most common complication after liner exchange.
In patients in whom the locking mechanism is damaged, a new liner can be cemented in place;
however, cemented liners are biomechanically inferior to those engaged in the locking
mechanism under certain stresses.

Nonpolyethylene Wear and Osteolysis
Wear is universal regardless of the material used and is not exclusive to polyethylene;
however, osteolysis should be considered a rare occurrence with these bearing surfaces.46
Ceramic on ceramic
Wear debris from ceramic bearings are produced in a bimodal distribution. Particles are
nanometric (5 to 90 nm) or micrometric (0.05 to 3.2 μm). These particles result in a limited
biologic response that occurs infrequently and only at high concentrations (Figure 2).

Metal on metal
Metal-on-metal articulations generate low volumes of wear debris. The estimated wear rate
is 2 μm per year. Metalloprotein complexes can produce a substantial inflammatory
response, which may result in osteolysis. The immune response to metal debris classically
differs from that to polyethylene debris.
A pattern of perivascular lymphocytic infiltration along with an accumulation of macrophages
and plasma cells has been observed and is typical of a failed metal-on-metal bearing.
Conversely, metal-on-polyethylene bearings do not produce the same pattern of lymphocytic
infiltration or the accumulation of plasma cells47,53 (Figure 3).
